result.summary: The Hesperides, turned into trees, tell the Argonauts where Heracles struck water from a rock, and the crew searches for him; Canthus and Mopsus die in Libya. With Triton's guidance Argo leaves the lake, Medea destroys the bronze giant Talos on Crete, and Apollo saves them from darkness at Anaphe. Euphemus's clod becomes the island Thera, and the crew sails home to Pagasae.

scenes.title: The Hesperides and the spring
scenes.summary: The nymphs become trees and tell of Heracles, who made water gush from a rock. The Minyae crowd the spring and praise him.
scenes.stakes: The crew are worn out with thirst and may die without water.

place.name: Garden of the Hesperides, near the Tritonian lake

scenes.title: Search for Heracles; deaths in Libya
scenes.summary: Scouts search for Heracles in vain. Canthus is killed by Caphaurus, and Mopsus dies of a serpent's bite; both are buried.
scenes.stakes: Canthus and Mopsus lose their lives.

scenes.title: Triton guides Argo out
scenes.summary: Orpheus has the tripod offered, and Triton gives Euphemus a clod and directions. He then tows Argo out to sea.
scenes.stakes: The crew are trapped in the lake with no way out.

scenes.title: Medea fells Talos
scenes.summary: On Crete the bronze man Talos blocks the landing. Medea bewitches him, and he wounds his ankle and falls.
scenes.stakes: The exhausted crew risk being driven off or crushed by Talos.

scenes.title: Darkness, Anaphe and Thera
scenes.summary: A black night falls and Apollo reveals the island Anaphe. Euphemus's dream leads to the clod becoming Calliste (Thera).
scenes.stakes: The crew are lost in total darkness at sea.

scenes.title: Home to Pagasae
scenes.summary: They stop at Aegina, then sail home without trouble to Pagasae.

analysis.text: The homeward journey closes the epic with divine help and the founding of colonies, showing the heroes' passing through the edges of the known world.
The Euphemus clod and Thera story gives a mythic origin for the Greek colonization of Thera and Cyrene.

legacy.text: Talos appears as a bronze giant in the film Jason and the Argonauts (1963), with effects by Ray Harryhausen.

fun_facts.text: The island Anaphe's name is explained by the poet through the Greek verb for 'to reveal', a typical Apollonian etiology.

language_notes.text: "So he spake" refers to Orpheus, who has just prayed to the nymphs for help; "lo!" introduces the sudden marvel that follows.
"Succour" means help or relief; "accursed" is the nymphs' bitter label for Heracles, who killed their serpent and took the apples.
"Fell" means cruel or fierce; "wanton violence" means reckless, unprovoked brutality.
The "bow of olive" probably means a club of olive wood, Heracles' famous weapon; the repeated "bow" seems confused, so the line reads awkwardly.
The Tritonian lake is the Libyan lake near which the Argonauts have been stranded; it is named for Triton, a sea god.
"Maw" is the stomach or gullet of a voracious animal, here used for Heracles' huge thirst.
"Fordone" is archaic for exhausted or worn out.
"That hero" is Heracles, who left the Argo's crew and founded a city (Cius) in Mysia after Hylas vanished; the Chalybes lived far east on the Black Sea.
The poet turns to address Canthus directly in the second person, "thee," an apostrophe typical of epic narration.
"The gods' heavy load" means Acacallis was pregnant by Phoebus (Apollo); Minos, her father, drove her out for it.
Paeeon is the divine healer of the gods, later identified with Apollo; the poet apologizes for suggesting even he could not cure the bite.
Perseus carried Medusa's severed head over Libya; drops of her blood were said to become serpents. Eurymedon was an alternate name given him by his mother.
The text names Canthus here, but Canthus is already dead; the bitten man is Mopsus, so this is a textual slip.
Marching thrice round the tomb in armour is a funeral rite honoring a dead warrior.
Propitiation means an offering meant to win the favour of gods and secure their goodwill.
"Farswaying" is a compound epithet describing Triton, perhaps meaning that his power shakes or sways the distant sea.
Offering a clod of earth was a token of hospitality and, as later events suggest, a symbol of granting possession of the land.
Apis and the sea of Minos are old names for the Peloponnese and the Cretan sea, the heroes' route home.
"Trends to the north" means the coast runs northward; they should follow it until it turns away, then steer straight on from the cape.
Phoreys and Nereus are other old sea-gods; Jason is unsure which name suits the god, so he covers all of them.
"The star that bids the shepherd fold" is the evening star, a poetic way of saying dusk had come.
"Men sprung from ash-trees" refers to the Bronze Age race of men, born from ash trees in Greek myth, as told by Hesiod.
"Issues of life and death" means the vein held his life; if it were cut, he would die.
The Death-spirits (Keres) are spirits of violent death, here called hounds of Hades, god of the underworld.
Ichor is the divine fluid that flows in the veins of gods and godlike beings instead of blood.
"Pall of Darkness" names a funeral-cloth image; the poet says the dark may be chaos from heaven or something rising from the underworld.
Pytho (Delphi), Amyclae and Ortygia (Delos) were major cult sites of Apollo, so Jason promises offerings at his chief shrines.
The narrator suddenly addresses Apollo directly as "son of Leto", shifting from third person to second.
Anaphe sounds like a Greek word meaning "revealed"; the poet gives an etymology for the island's name, as he does for Apollo's title "Gleamer" (Aigletes).
The handmaids were given to Medea by Alcinous in Phaeacia, where sacrifices were lavish; the bare offerings here seemed laughably poor.
The poet ties the scene to a living ritual on Anaphe, in which women mock the men during sacrifice, an aition (origin story).
"Son of Maia" is Hermes; Euphemus reveres him presumably because the clod's dream-giver was a god, so the dream is taken as sacred.
"Far-Darter" is an epithet of Apollo, the archer god; Jason reads the dream as prophecy.
This compresses the history of Euphemus's descendants and the colonization of Thera (Santorini) by Theras, which later led to the founding of Cyrene.
Myrmidons were the people of Aegina and later of Achilles; the water-carrying race is a local custom explained by the Argonauts' contest.

context_notes.text: Hespere, Eretheis and Aegle are the Hesperides, nymphs of the west who guarded the golden apples with the serpent Ladon.
Heracles' eleventh labor was to fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides; he killed the guardian serpent and left shortly before the Argonauts arrived.
The untanned lion skin is Heracles' trademark garment, taken from the Nemean lion he killed in an earlier labor.
The sons of Boreas, Zetes and Calais, were winged; Lynceus was famed for sight so keen he could see underground, and Euphemus for running swiftly.
Mopsus was a seer son of Ampycus, who had prophesied for the Argonauts; his death shows that prophecy cannot avert fate.
The Argonauts had carried Argo overland to Lake Tritonis in Libya after storms drove them off course, so they must now find the lake's outlet.
Triton is a sea-god, son of Poseidon, usually shown as part man and part fish.
Aeson's son is Jason, the leader of the expedition.
Europa was a Phoenician princess carried to Crete by Jove (Zeus), who gave her this bronze guardian to protect the island.
Aeson's son is Jason, leader of the Argonauts and Medea's partner; Medea veils her face as she begins her dark magic.
Minoan Athena is Athena worshipped in Crete, where the Argonauts had just landed.
Triton is a sea god, and Libya his consort here; the clod was his gift to Euphemus on the Libyan coast.
The poet lists the Greek coast the Argonauts passed on the way back, ending at Pagasae, where the ship Argo was launched.

literary_notes.text: The nymphs turn into trees, a transformation common in Greek myth, rewarding the Argonauts' prayer with a visible marvel.
Comparing Heracles to a beast stooping to drink stresses his raw, animal strength and overwhelming thirst.
The Minyae crowding the spring are compared to ants and flies at honey, a small and slightly comic image of their desperate thirst.
Heracles saves his comrades although absent and unaware, and he had earlier been left behind by them.
"The doom of the gods" hints that Canthus's eager search will end in his death.
Lynceus's faint, uncertain sight of Heracles is compared to glimpsing the new moon through cloud, conveying how dim and distant the vision is.
The narrator addresses the dead Canthus directly, heightening pathos and marking his death as a solemn moment.
"Poor wretch!" is a narrator's exclamation inviting sympathy as the poison's slow numbness is described.
The ship's aimless wandering is compared to a heat-maddened snake twisting about until it finds its hole, conveying frustration and the search for an exit.
Triton's sudden, unseen disappearance hints that the helper was divine, a fact the narrator confirms in later sentences.
Triton guiding Argo is likened to a man leading a proud horse by the mane, making the god's strength seem gentle and controlled.
The vivid description of Triton's human torso, forked tail and crescent-like fins makes the marvel visible and explains the heroes' awe.
The detail of the single covered vein, his weak point, prepares for his downfall through the ankle.
The narrator breaks off to address Father Zeus directly, voicing his own astonishment at Medea's power to harm from afar.
Talos's fall is compared to a half-cut pine toppling at last, conveying his slow swaying and the huge crash.
The starless, moonless darkness is rendered as physical chaos, creating terror and a sense of cosmic disorientation.
Apollo's golden bow flashing light across the sea is a vivid contrast to the preceding blackness, signaling divine rescue.
The clod suckled by milk and turning into a woman symbolizes the future colony: earth becoming a nurturing homeland for Euphemus's descendants.
The narrator turns to address the heroes directly, blessing them and marking the poem's approaching end.
The poet speaks in the first person, announcing the end of his labor and summarizing the quiet voyage home.
